title: The daily mental routine
teaches: Run the trading day in three parts: a warm-up before the open (game plan, levels, your own state, if-then rules), breaks and check-ins during the session, and a written cool-down after the close that picks one thing to improve tomorrow.

facts.quote: Notice how in most performance activities, top performers engage in warm up exercises. Singers, musicians, athletes--all have their warm up routines.
facts.claim: In most performance fields, top performers warm up before they perform.

facts.quote: Your trading warm up should put you in the mental, physical, and emotional state you need to be in to do your best trading.
facts.claim: A trading warm-up readies your mind, body and emotions, not just your charts.

facts.quote: Many, many trading problems occur simply because the right functions were never warmed up.
facts.claim: Many trading problems start because the trader never warmed up.

facts.quote: I love to mentally rehearse different market scenarios as we approach the open. The scenarios include how I would respond to early weakness or strength
facts.claim: Before the open, Steenbarger rehearses how he would respond to early weakness or strength.

facts.quote: Warm ups practice the functions we most want to employ.
facts.claim: A warm-up practises the skills you are about to use.

facts.quote: Contemplating many market possibilities helps ensure I don't get locked into any one.
facts.claim: Rehearsing several scenarios keeps you from getting locked into one view.

facts.quote: Review before trading starts to ensure that the rules are being followed in generating ideas, with special emphasis on the rules relevant to the prior day's trading;
facts.claim: Steenbarger reviews his written rules before trading starts.

facts.quote: Review at the end of trading to assess whether rules were followed and especially to look at how a following of the rules could have improved the day's trading;
facts.claim: At the end of the trading day he checks whether he followed his rules.

facts.quote: Targeting one or more rules to focus on for the coming session to improve trading.
facts.claim: He then picks a rule or two to focus on in the next session.

facts.quote: What if, at any given time, we worked on one goal and one goal only. Suppose we worked on it every single day and made it the focus on each day's efforts.
facts.claim: Steenbarger suggests working on one goal at a time, every day.

facts.quote: By setting a large number of goals, traders have difficulties prioritizing the changes they want to make, and they find it difficult to give each of the goals proper attention.
facts.claim: With too many goals, none of them gets proper attention.

facts.quote: A vague goal is only a good intention; it's not likely to energize or shape performance. My experience is that vague goals get the least follow-through.
facts.claim: Vague goals get the least follow-through.

facts.quote: Elite performers--in music, theater, professional sports, chess--spend more time practicing and preparing than actually performing in competition.
facts.claim: Elite performers spend more time practising and preparing than performing.

facts.quote: Trading without review is like playing a football game without huddles; like preparing for a baseball or basketball game without practices or review of game film.
facts.claim: Trading without review is like playing sport without practice or game film.

facts.quote: Ideas must include entries/stops/targets/risk amount
facts.claim: In an SMB trader's morning routine that Steenbarger published, every idea needs an entry, stop, target and risk amount.

facts.quote: If you're not working on change daily, you're not working on change. And if you try to accomplish massive changes in one day, you run the risk of activating competing motivations and derailing your efforts.
facts.claim: Change is a daily job, and trying to change everything at once tends to derail it.

facts.quote: But most of us are far from ideal and need to change one action at a time.
facts.claim: Steenbarger passes on a point he calls excellent: most of us need to change one action at a time.

facts.quote: The key to remaking yourself is to find the small steps that add to big changes without setting off alarms.
facts.claim: Small steps add up to big changes.

facts.quote: I find that a surprising proportion of what sets traders up for success during the day is what has happened the previous night.
facts.claim: Much of what sets up a good trading day happens the night before.

facts.quote: One study found that financial decision making was meaningfully impaired when subjects were sleepy due to poorer judgment about the task being undertaken.
facts.claim: Steenbarger cites a study in which sleepy people made worse financial decisions.

facts.quote: If we make decisions in cognitive, emotional, and physical states that are different from the ones we occupied during our preparation, we're likely to find that the decisions we plan won't always be the ones we act upon.
facts.claim: A plan made in one state won't always be the one you act on in a different state.

facts.quote: Preparation puts emotion into perspective; we gain control, not by staying Zen, but by anticipating situations that are likely to take us out of calm focus and preparing our responses to those.
facts.claim: You gain control by planning your response to the situations that throw you off.

facts.quote: We cannot--and should not--eliminate emotion from trading, but that is also not necessary.
facts.claim: The goal is not to have no emotion while trading.

facts.quote: At the end of the day, week, and month, you can track what you did well and what needs improvement.
facts.claim: Review at the end of each day, week and month: what went well and what needs work.

facts.quote: Both provide opportunities for goal setting, as you have goals to repeat and expand what you did well and goals to correct what you didn't do well.
facts.claim: What you did well becomes a goal to repeat; what you did badly becomes a goal to correct.

facts.quote: Note how in every performance activity--acting, music, sports, dancing--there are active practice sessions that accomplish two purposes: they keep the performer in shape, and they rehearse the challenges that are likely to be faced during live performance.
facts.claim: Every performance field has practice sessions that keep the performer in shape and rehearse live challenges.

facts.quote: The routines of trading are what enable us to process market information efficiently and stick to what we do best.
facts.claim: Routines let you process the market efficiently and stick to what you do best.

facts.quote: If you identify a best practice in your trading, the best thing you can do is transform it into a robust habit pattern. A definition of good trading could be: doing automatically what you would ideally do by choice.
facts.claim: Turn your best practices into habits, so you do the right thing automatically.

facts.quote: Routine is the friend of efficiency and the enemy of change.
facts.claim: Routines make you efficient but can stop you from changing.

facts.quote: There is a world of difference between the person with five years of experience and the person who repeats a year's experience five times.
facts.claim: Repeating the same year is not the same as growing for five years.

facts.quote: It's the reworking of old trading processes and the addition of new ones that enable traders to stay profitable when markets go from trending and non-volatile to volatile and choppy.
facts.claim: Reworking your processes is what keeps you profitable when markets turn choppy.

facts.quote: We act as if experience itself will teach us all we need to know, when it is guided experience--experience informed by goals and feedback--that gets us where we want to go.
facts.claim: Experience teaches best when it is guided by goals and feedback.

facts.quote: My trading day begins early in the morning with an assessment of overseas markets, an advance look at economic reports due for the day, a review of the prior day's market indicators
facts.claim: Steenbarger's trading day starts with overseas markets, the day's scheduled economic reports and yesterday's indicators.

facts.quote: We become fatigued, and in the fatigued state we're more likely to make mistakes and fall into old habit patterns that cost us money.
facts.claim: When you're fatigued, mistakes and old bad habits become more likely.

facts.quote: Either you battle test your plans in rehearsal mode or they will be tested in actual battle.
facts.claim: Rehearse your plan before the session, or the market will test it for you.

facts.quote: When we establish a routine--and then make it routine--we take our strengths and make them automatic.
facts.claim: A routine you keep turns your strengths into automatic habits.

facts.quote: If you are focused on small wins and the processes that generate profits over time, however, the coming week can always be a successful one.
facts.claim: Judge yourself on the process that makes money over time, not on one day's result.

facts.quote: When we study our successes and figure out how we are making use of our strengths at those times, we become able to define our best practices.
facts.claim: Studying your successes is how you find your best practices.

facts.quote: When it comes to your Mental Game, I typically focus on four major areas for winning routines: Daily Overall Routine Pre-Session Warm Up In-Session/Tournament Routine Post-Session Cool Down
facts.claim: Tendler's routine has four parts: the daily basics, a warm-up before, a routine during, and a cool-down after the session.

facts.quote: If your routines need improvement, start small. Look for just one thing you can add that can make a slight improvement.
facts.claim: Improve a routine one small addition at a time.

facts.quote: Your daily routine covers the basics: what and when you eat, exercise, recharge, and sleep.
facts.claim: The daily routine covers food, exercise, recharging and sleep.

facts.quote: Before you begin trading or playing poker, you need to get your mind ready – much like an athlete readies their body to compete.
facts.claim: Get your mind ready before you trade, the way an athlete readies the body.

facts.quote: Without this, you won't be sharp when you start and are at risk of mistakes or missing opportunities.
facts.claim: Skip the warm-up and you start dull, at risk of mistakes and missed chances.

facts.quote: For traders, that sometimes means reviewing overnight sessions, looking at stock screeners or TA levels, and gauging what symbols you are looking for that day.
facts.claim: The strategic part of the warm-up: overnight action, screens, levels and today's names.

facts.quote: Both traders and poker players should also include a mental game plan to address the problems that are most likely to affect you – such as tilt, boredom, focus
facts.claim: The warm-up includes a plan for the mental problems most likely to hit you.

facts.quote: My best advice here is to not wait until you need it. Find your trend, or key on early warning signs, so you can take a break before your energy nosedives.
facts.claim: Take a break before your energy drops, not after.

facts.quote: But fatigue decreases your ability to control your emotions and emotional volatility increases your chances of making a mistake.
facts.claim: Fatigue weakens emotional control, and that raises the odds of a mistake.

facts.quote: What you do after the session or event is all about tomorrow.
facts.claim: The cool-down is preparation for tomorrow.

facts.quote: Sometimes we rely too much on our memory. As soon as you walk away, details start to disappear.
facts.claim: Details fade as soon as you walk away, so write them down.

facts.quote: On days where there was some significant emotion, the goal is to reduce the chance of that emotion carrying over to the following day.
facts.claim: After an emotional day, the cool-down aims to stop the emotion carrying into tomorrow.

facts.quote: At a minimum, do a brain dump, writing out everything in your mind, what happened, what the emotion was, what the trigger was
facts.claim: At minimum, write out what happened, what you felt and what triggered it.

facts.quote: While they don't guarantee that you will perform at your best, they do make it more likely.
facts.claim: Routines don't guarantee your best performance; they make it more likely.

facts.quote: Obviously there are no guarantees that winning routines will translate into winning results, but they definitely increase the probability
facts.claim: Good routines raise the odds of good results, with no guarantee.

facts.quote: If you don't, the chance you will make the same mistake again goes up and nothing is more frustrating than making the same mistake over and over.
facts.claim: Skip the cool-down and you are more likely to repeat the same mistake.

facts.quote: What did you do well in general and/or improve on the things you've been working on? What mistakes did you make? How can you improve on them and/or be better next time?
facts.claim: Tendler's three cool-down questions: what went well, what mistakes you made, how to improve next time.

facts.quote: You need to get the emotion out and the best time to do it is soon after you're done.
facts.claim: The best time to process a session's emotion is soon after it ends.

facts.quote: To create your bubble, write for up to 15 minutes, one hour before you start to play/trade.
facts.claim: Before trading, write out what's on your mind for up to 15 minutes.

facts.quote: This gives you an opportunity to get some of the emotion out and/or make a list of tasks, with the intent of being able to put them away for now.
facts.claim: Writing it out lets you put outside worries away for the session.

facts.quote: you go through waves where you do it regularly, only to fall off during periods when you're doing quite well, evidence of some subtle overconfidence weakening your process.
facts.claim: Dropping the journal when things go well is a sign of subtle overconfidence.

facts.quote: the idea is to eventually reach the point where it's so ingrained as part of your daily routine that you can't not do it.
facts.claim: The aim is a habit so ingrained you do it without forcing it.

facts.quote: when you're tired, or burnt out, your emotions get bigger while your ability to deal with them is more limited.
facts.claim: Tired, your emotions grow and your ability to handle them shrinks.

facts.quote: Traders should at least have written "if, then" plans to help limit emotion-based actions and prevent additional big losses and should consciously commit to these plans before every trading session.
facts.claim: Write if-then plans and commit to them before every session.

facts.quote: For example, they could pledge to step away for the day if they lose a certain amount of money or take 15 minutes if they feel an urge to break a trading rule.
facts.claim: Examples: stop for the day after a set loss, or take 15 minutes when you feel the urge to break a rule.

facts.quote: Writing about worries before a high-pressure event frees up working memory, allowing more capacity to focus on the task at hand.
facts.claim: Writing out worries before a high-pressure event frees attention for the task.

facts.quote: If a trader mentally practices the ideal response to certain situations, it should help them execute when those situations arise for real.
facts.claim: Mentally practising your response helps you carry it out for real.

facts.quote: Studies have consistently linked intense emotional reactions to poor trading performance.
facts.claim: Intense emotional reactions go with poor trading performance.

facts.quote: Psychological studies suggest that when athletes write about performance failures, it can reduce the mental impact and help them reframe the event as a set of lessons instead.
facts.claim: Writing about a failure can soften its impact and turn it into lessons.

facts.quote: Whatever the reason for the blowup, traders can get past it, but positive thinking alone won't do the trick.
facts.claim: Positive thinking alone does not fix a trading problem.

facts.quote: If a trader has trouble distancing their emotions from their trading decisions, it's never a bad idea to slow down or even take a break. Cooler heads usually prevail, and trading is no exception.
facts.claim: When emotion creeps into decisions, slow down or take a break.

facts.quote: Even seasoned traders can find buying and selling near the opening and closing bells a bit like surfing when waves are biggest—if they misread the conditions, they might get hurt.
facts.claim: Trading near the open is hard even for experienced traders.

facts.quote: But when news breaks outside of trading hours, an imbalance between buy and sell orders may cause a stock to open dramatically higher or lower than its price at the previous close.
facts.claim: News outside trading hours can make a stock open far from its prior close.

facts.quote: Trading in the market is about probabilities, not certainties.
facts.claim: Trading is about probabilities, not certainties.

facts.quote: Don't play it by ear—you must have some pre-fixed levels in your mind for every stock you plan to trade.
facts.claim: Set your levels in advance for every stock you plan to trade.

facts.quote: But as a novice, it is better to just read the market without making any moves for the first 15–20 minutes.
facts.claim: Investopedia suggests novices watch the open for the first 15 to 20 minutes before acting.

facts.quote: knowing the latest in the stock markets, keeping track of events that affect stocks
facts.claim: Keep track of the events that move stocks.

facts.quote: Update your trading plan weekly or monthly to include new ideas and eliminate bad ones.
facts.claim: Revise your plan regularly: add what works, drop what doesn't.

facts.quote: Don't try to make up for a losing trade by trading more. Revenge trading is a recipe for disaster.
facts.claim: Don't trade more to win back a loss.

facts.quote: Stay away from stock boards and chat rooms, where people are less than serious and many of them have ulterior motives.
facts.claim: Stay away from stock boards and chat rooms.

facts.quote: Discipline can't be taught in a seminar or found in expensive trading software.
facts.claim: Discipline doesn't come from software or seminars.

facts.quote: The only way to achieve long-term success is with hard work and discipline.
facts.claim: Long-term success comes from hard work and discipline.

facts.quote: We find that subjects whose emotional reaction to monetary gains and losses was more intense on both the positive and negative side exhibited significantly worse trading performance.
facts.claim: Traders with stronger emotional reactions to both gains and losses traded significantly worse.

facts.quote: We investigate several possible links between psychological factors and trading performance in a sample of 80 anonymous day-traders.
facts.claim: The study followed 80 day traders.

facts.quote: If trading is indeed a performance field, there is no reason to believe that elite performance will be found in better indicators, faster or more comprehensive software, newsletter tips, or coaching advice.
facts.claim: If trading is a performance field, elite performance won't come from better tools or tips.

facts.quote: Only a directed developmental process will allow you to internalize market patterns and act upon these with confidence.
facts.claim: Only directed development lets you learn market patterns and act on them with confidence.

facts.quote: In sum, my best advice is to truly treat trading as a profession if it is to be your career.
facts.claim: Steenbarger and Toghraie's advice: treat trading as a profession.

facts.quote: Better golf clubs will not turn a duffer into a pro; the finest wrenches will not make one a master mechanic.
facts.claim: Better tools don't make a professional.

facts.quote: Core Trading Session: 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. ET
facts.claim: The NYSE core session runs from 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. ET.

facts.quote: Take your time and don't ever invest in anything you haven't thoroughly and independently researched.
facts.claim: Never buy anything you haven't researched yourself.

walkthroughs.title: Trading is a performance
steps: Singers, musicians and athletes all warm up before they perform. Coach Brett Steenbarger wants you to do the same.
Treat trading as a profession. Elite performers spend more time preparing than performing.
So your trading day has three parts: warm up, trade, cool down.

walkthroughs.title: Before the open
steps: Start with the game plan: today's names, the levels, and an entry and stop for each.
Then check the trader. How you slept, what's on your mind, which mistake is most likely today.
Write an if-then rule for that mistake, like stepping away after a set loss. Commit to it before the bell.

walkthroughs.title: During and after
steps: During the session, trade the plan. Take short breaks before you're drained, not after.
After the close, write it up while it's fresh: what went well, what went wrong, what to do better.
Then pick one thing to work on tomorrow. One thing, and specific. Small daily steps add up.

questions.q: Top singers, musicians and athletes share one habit before they perform. Steenbarger wants traders to copy it. What is it?
choices: They warm up first
They start cold and find a rhythm
They follow a lucky ritual
questions.why: They warm up first. Steenbarger points out that singers, musicians and athletes all have warm-up routines. Tendler says the same for trading: get your mind ready the way an athlete readies the body.
questions.lesson_line: Nobody serious performs cold. Warm up before the open.

wrong.They start cold and find a rhythm: That makes your first trades the warm-up. Tendler: without one, you're not sharp at the start and you risk mistakes.
wrong.They follow a lucky ritual: A ritual for luck has no job to do. Steenbarger's warm-up practises the exact skills you're about to use.

questions.q: Tendler and Steenbarger both build the trading day in the same order. Which order is it?
choices: Warm up, trade, cool down
Trade first, warm up as you go
Warm up, trade, then log off
questions.why: Warm up, trade, cool down. Tendler's routine has a warm-up before the session and a cool-down after it. Steenbarger reviews his rules before trading starts and again at the end of the day.
questions.lesson_line: Three parts, every day: before the open, during the session, after the close.

wrong.Trade first, warm up as you go: Then the market is your warm-up, and it charges for it. The warm-up comes before your first order.
wrong.Warm up, trade, then log off: That skips the review. Tendler says what you do after the session is all about tomorrow.

questions.q: A good warm-up is all charts and levels. Your own head can wait until the bell.
questions.why: False. Steenbarger's warm-up should put you in the mental, physical and emotional state to do your best trading. Tendler adds a plan for the problems most likely to hit you, like tilt or losing focus.
questions.lesson_line: Warm up the trader, not just the watchlist.

questions.q: Which job belongs in your warm-up before the open?
choices: Levels, entry and stop per name
Scan chat rooms for the hot tips
Wait and decide once it opens
questions.answer: Levels, entry and stop per name
questions.why: Levels, entry and stop per name. Tendler's warm-up covers the levels and the names you're watching that day. An SMB trader's morning plan, shared by Steenbarger, needs an entry, stop, target and risk amount for every idea.
questions.lesson_line: Every name on today's list gets its levels before the bell.

wrong.Scan chat rooms for the hot tips: Hot tips are someone else's idea, not your plan. Investopedia warns that on stock boards and chat rooms, many have ulterior motives.
wrong.Wait and decide once it opens: That's playing it by ear. Investopedia's rule: have set levels in mind for every stock you plan to trade.

questions.q: Your trading routine starts the night before, with how you sleep.
questions.why: True. Steenbarger finds a surprising share of what sets up a good trading day happens the night before. Tendler's daily routine covers the basics: food, exercise, recharging and sleep.
questions.lesson_line: Tomorrow's warm-up starts with tonight's sleep.

questions.q: Steenbarger treats trading as a performance field, like sport or music. In that view, what builds top performance?
choices: Directed practice and review
A sharper set of chart indicators
Newsletter tips and alerts
questions.why: Directed practice and review. Steenbarger notes that every performance field uses practice sessions to rehearse the challenges of live performance. In a Fidelity piece, he and Adrienne Toghraie add that elite performance won't come from better indicators, software or tips.
questions.lesson_line: Train like an athlete: prepare, perform, review. Better tools don't replace the reps.

wrong.A sharper set of chart indicators: Steenbarger and Toghraie: better golf clubs won't turn a duffer into a pro. Tools help, but practice builds the skill.
wrong.Newsletter tips and alerts: Tips are someone else's thinking. Steenbarger and Toghraie list them among the things that won't create elite performance.

questions.q: Finish the line.
questions.sentence: When your routine needs work, add ___ new thing at a time.
questions.why: One. Tendler: when your routines need work, start small and look for just one thing to add. Steenbarger's version: work on one goal at a time, every day.
questions.lesson_line: One small change you keep beats a big overhaul you drop.

questions.q: Steenbarger has a one-line definition of good trading that explains why routines matter. Which is it?
choices: Doing the ideal thing automatically
Never feeling any fear or any greed
Taking every setup the market gives you
questions.why: Doing the ideal thing automatically. Steenbarger: good trading could be 'doing automatically what you would ideally do by choice'. Tendler wants the same from a habit: so ingrained you can't not do it.
questions.lesson_line: Repeat the right steps until you no longer need the checklist.

wrong.Never feeling any fear or any greed: Steenbarger says we can't, and shouldn't, remove emotion from trading. The routine works with it.
wrong.Taking every setup the market gives you: That's overtrading. A routine narrows the day to the setups you planned.

questions.q: Your names, levels and stops are set. What else do you check before the open?
choices: News and reports due today
Nothing, levels are enough
Where the market will close
questions.why: News and reports due today. Steenbarger's morning includes an advance look at the economic reports due that day. Investopedia's rules include keeping track of the events that affect stocks.
questions.lesson_line: Know what's on the calendar before the bell, not when it hits.

wrong.Nothing, levels are enough: News that breaks outside trading hours can make a stock open far above or below its last close. Know what's coming.
wrong.Where the market will close: Nobody knows that. The warm-up covers what's scheduled and how you'll respond, not a forecast.

questions.story: You know your pattern. After a losing trade, you rush into the next one. Today's charts and levels are ready.
questions.q: What should your warm-up add?
choices: An if-then rule for after a loss
Nothing, the charts are all set
A reminder to stay positive today
questions.answer: An if-then rule for after a loss
questions.why: An if-then rule for after a loss. Tendler's warm-up includes a plan for the problems most likely to hit you. Schwab suggests written if-then plans, committed to before every session. One example: take 15 minutes when you feel an urge to break a rule.
questions.lesson_line: Know your pattern. Write the rule for it before the bell, not after the damage.

wrong.Nothing, the charts are all set: The charts are set. The trader isn't. A pattern you already know needs a plan too.
wrong.A reminder to stay positive today: Schwab: positive thinking alone won't do the trick. You need a specific response, decided in advance.

questions.q: Before the open, Steenbarger rehearses how he'd respond to early strength or weakness. What's the point of rehearsing?
choices: To follow your plan when it gets real
To forecast where the market will open
To find more reasons to take trades
questions.answer: To follow your plan when it gets real
questions.why: To follow your plan when it gets real. Steenbarger: decisions you plan in one state won't always be the ones you act on in another. Schwab says practising the ideal response helps you carry it out for real.
questions.lesson_line: Rehearse the response before the bell, so the market isn't your first test.

wrong.To forecast where the market will open: Rehearsal isn't a forecast. Steenbarger runs through many scenarios so he doesn't get locked into any one.
wrong.To find more reasons to take trades: Rehearsal is about how you respond, not how often you trade.

questions.q: Finish Tendler's three cool-down questions.
questions.sentence: What did I do well? What mistakes did I make? How can I ___ next time?
questions.why: Improve. Tendler's three questions: what you did well, what mistakes you made, and how to improve on them next time. Steenbarger's review tracks what you did well and what needs improvement.
questions.lesson_line: Three questions after every session: what worked, what didn't, what changes tomorrow.

questions.q: Getting very excited after wins is harmless. Only the sting after losses hurts your trading.
questions.why: False. In a study of 80 day traders, those with more intense emotional reactions to gains and to losses traded significantly worse. Schwab notes studies consistently link intense emotion to poor trading.
questions.lesson_line: Check in after wins too. A big high is a warning sign, just like a big low.

questions.story: A fight with your landlord is still on your mind. The open is an hour away.
questions.q: What does Tendler suggest before you trade?
choices: Write it out, then set it aside
Push it down and focus on charts
Trade to take your mind off it
questions.answer: Write it out, then set it aside
questions.why: Write it out, then set it aside. Tendler suggests writing for up to 15 minutes before you trade, to get it out and put it away for now. Schwab notes that writing about worries before a big moment frees up working memory.
questions.lesson_line: Get it on paper, then draw a line under it. It waits until after the close.

wrong.Push it down and focus on charts: Pushed down, it keeps pulling at your attention. Writing it out frees that attention for the market.
wrong.Trade to take your mind off it: That puts money on a distracted mind. A trade is not a way to stop thinking about something else.

questions.story: It's 11:30 a.m. You were sharp all morning. Now you're rereading the same chart and snapping at small things.
questions.q: What does a good in-session routine say?
choices: Take a short break now
Push through to the close
Trade more to get your edge back
questions.why: Take a short break now. Tendler says don't wait until you need one: fatigue cuts your control over emotions and raises your odds of a mistake. Schwab agrees: slow down or even take a break.
questions.lesson_line: Breaks are part of the plan. Take one before you're running on empty.

wrong.Push through to the close: Steenbarger: in a fatigued state you're more likely to make mistakes and slip into old habits that cost money.
wrong.Trade more to get your edge back: More trades from a tired mind means more chances for the mistakes fatigue brings.

questions.q: Writing up today's trades on the weekend works as well as writing them up right after the close.
questions.why: False. Tendler: as soon as you walk away, details start to disappear. The best time to get the emotion out is soon after you're done. Steenbarger reviews at the end of each trading day.
questions.lesson_line: Write it while it's fresh. By the weekend, many details are gone.

questions.story: You overslept. It's 9:25 a.m. ET, and the open is at 9:30. No warm-up, no levels, and a stock you've never studied is ripping premarket.
questions.q: What's the move?
choices: Hold off until your prep is done
Buy the runner before it gets away
Trade your normal size, prep later
questions.answer: Hold off until your prep is done
questions.why: Hold off until your prep is done. Without a warm-up, Tendler says you're not sharp and you risk mistakes. Investor.gov's advice fits too: don't ever invest in anything you haven't researched.
questions.lesson_line: No prep, no trade yet. Let the open go and get your plan back first.

wrong.Buy the runner before it gets away: No levels, no stop, no research. Schwab notes even seasoned traders can get hurt trading near the opening bell.
wrong.Trade your normal size, prep later: Prep later means trading unprepared now. Steenbarger: many trading problems start because the right skills were never warmed up.

questions.story: Ugly day. You moved your stop, took a big loss, and you're angry. It's 4:10 p.m. and you want to shut the laptop.
questions.q: What's your cool-down tonight?
choices: Write out what happened and why
Shut it, forget it, start fresh
Trade after hours to win it back
questions.answer: Write out what happened and why
questions.why: Write out what happened and why. On an emotional day, Tendler's goal is to keep the emotion from carrying over to tomorrow. At minimum, a brain dump: what happened, what you felt, what set it off.
questions.lesson_line: Bad days need the cool-down most. Get it on paper before you sleep.

wrong.Shut it, forget it, start fresh: Tendler: skip the cool-down and the odds of making the same mistake again go up.
wrong.Trade after hours to win it back: That's revenge trading. Investopedia's rules call it a recipe for disaster.

questions.story: Your review lists six fixes: entries, stops, size, sleep, focus and patience. You want all six fixed by tomorrow.
questions.q: What goal do you set for tomorrow?
choices: One fix, stated specifically
Work on all six fixes at once
Just be more disciplined
No goal, trade and see
questions.why: One fix, stated specifically. Steenbarger finds too many goals scatter your attention, and vague goals get the least follow-through. Tendler says the same: start small, one thing at a time.
questions.lesson_line: One goal, specific enough to check tonight. Then the next one.

wrong.Work on all six fixes at once: Too many goals, and none gets proper attention. Steenbarger works one goal at a time, every day.
wrong.Just be more disciplined: That's a good intention, not a goal. You can't check it at the close.
wrong.No goal, trade and see: Experience alone teaches slowly. Steenbarger: guided experience, with goals and feedback, is what gets you there.

questions.q: You ran your routine perfectly and still lost money today. That means the routine is broken.
questions.why: False. Tendler: routines don't guarantee results, they raise the odds. Schwab: trading is about probabilities, not certainties. Judge the routine by the process over time, not by one day.
questions.lesson_line: One red day says little about a good routine. Judge it over weeks.

questions.story: Best week of your year. Friday afternoon you skip the review. Things are clearly working.
questions.q: Is skipping it a problem?
choices: Yes, good weeks hold lessons to repeat
No, reviews are for losing weeks
No, but raise your size next week
questions.answer: Yes, good weeks hold lessons to repeat
questions.why: Yes. Good weeks hold lessons to repeat. Steenbarger turns what you did well into goals to repeat and expand. Tendler warns that dropping the journal when things go well is a sign of subtle overconfidence.
questions.lesson_line: Review the great weeks too. That's where you learn what to repeat.

wrong.No, reviews are for losing weeks: Steenbarger: studying your successes is how you define your best practices.
wrong.No, but raise your size next week: That's the overconfidence Tendler warns about. A hot streak is when the process quietly slips.

questions.story: You slept badly and skipped your warm-up. Ten minutes after the open, your first trade is a loss. You want right back in.
questions.q: What's the right call?
choices: Step away and do the warm-up now
Jump back in to make it back
Keep trading, tighten every stop
questions.answer: Step away and do the warm-up now
questions.why: Step away and do the warm-up now. Tendler: when you're tired, your emotions get bigger and you have less to handle them with. Schwab's if-then plans include taking 15 minutes when you feel an urge to break a rule.
questions.lesson_line: When the day starts wrong, reset first. The next setup can wait for you.

wrong.Jump back in to make it back: That's revenge trading. Investopedia: don't try to make up for a losing trade by trading more.
wrong.Keep trading, tighten every stop: A tighter stop doesn't fix a tired, rattled mind. The problem is the trader, not the stop.

questions.story: Same routine for two years. The market has gone from smooth trends to choppy swings. Your results have gone flat.
questions.q: What does Steenbarger suggest?
choices: Rework the routine, keep what works
Stick with it, since it worked before
Drop routines and trade on feel
questions.answer: Rework the routine, keep what works
questions.why: Rework the routine, keep what works. Steenbarger: routine is the friend of efficiency and the enemy of change. Reworking old processes is what keeps traders profitable when markets turn choppy.
questions.lesson_line: Keep the routine, but review it. When the market changes, your prep changes too.

wrong.Stick with it, since it worked before: Steenbarger: there's a world of difference between five years of experience and one year repeated five times.
wrong.Drop routines and trade on feel: That throws out what works with what doesn't. Routines are what let you process the market efficiently.

conflicts: Tier 1 is thin for this topic: no SEC, FINRA or exchange page describes a trader's daily mental routine. The file rests on two independent named authors (Steenbarger's TraderFeed, Tendler's own site) plus Schwab, Investopedia and NBER. Every key has at least two of those publishers, or a Tier 1 fact (q17: Investor.gov, NYSE).

Steenbarger appears through three publishers: TraderFeed (his blog), Fidelity (a 2011 piece he co-wrote with Adrienne Toghraie, adapted from both their Wiley books) and NBER (a study he co-wrote). No key rests only on Steenbarger sources: every Steenbarger-led key also cites Tendler, Schwab or Investopedia (q06 pairs TraderFeed and the Fidelity piece with Investopedia's 'discipline can't be ... found in expensive trading software'; q13 pairs NBER with Schwab). Checker 2026-11-09: the Fidelity page does not say which author wrote which line, so q06 and w1 no longer credit its lines to Steenbarger alone.

Investor.gov 'Thinking of Day Trading? Know the Risks.' (s41) is a former Director's Take, marked on the page as no longer being updated. It is cited only for the timeless line 'don't ever invest in anything you haven't thoroughly and independently researched' (q17), next to Tendler and Investopedia.

Steenbarger's 2016 recovery post (s13) says willpower 'runs out of power'. Willpower depletion ('ego depletion') is a contested finding in psychology. The file cites only the post's fatigue line (fatigue makes mistakes and old habits more likely, which Tendler also says) and never keys willpower depletion.
Steenbarger's 2014 post 'Priming as Performance Preparation' builds on behavioural priming, another finding with replication problems. Not used.

Tendler's 'Building a Winning Routine' mentions 'around eight hours of sleep'. Sleep amounts are a health claim outside this unit; the file teaches only that sleep is part of the routine (Steenbarger + Tendler), with no number.

Investopedia (s33) suggests a novice 'read the market without making any moves for the first 15-20 minutes'. That is a day-trading tip for beginners, cited in q17 only as support that holding off at the open is legitimate; it is never keyed as a rule.

NBER w11243 (s35) is one study of 80 day traders and is correlational. q13 says 'in a study of 80 day traders' and keys only what the abstract states (more intense reactions on both sides went with significantly worse performance), alongside Schwab's 'studies have consistently linked intense emotional reactions to poor trading performance'.

The SMB trader's morning list (s5, fact fe2) is one trader's own routine as published by Steenbarger. q04 uses it as an example ('an SMB trader's morning plan'), with Tendler and Investopedia for the key.

The unit plan's 'covers' column points to uct-intelligence/prompts/06_psychology.txt S5 and 'examples needed' to app/src/constants/quotes.json.
